problems.name: Collins–Shor conjecture on the peak of the distance characteristic polynomial of a tree

source.citation: G. Aalipour, A. Abiad, Z. Berikkyzy, L. Hogben, F. H. J. Kenter, J. C.-H. Lin, M. Tait, Proof of a conjecture of Graham and Lovász concerning unimodality of coefficients of the distance characteristic polynomial of a tree, arXiv:1507.02341, Conjecture 1.2 (journal version: Electron. J. Linear Algebra 34:373-380, 2018, according to the reference lists of arXiv:2206.07561 and arXiv:2407.03309; not checked against the journal); originally Conjecture 9 of K. L. Collins, On a conjecture of Graham and Lovász about distance matrices, Discrete Appl. Math. 25 (1989) 27-35, attributed there to P. Shor.
source.note: The catalogued wording is Conjecture 1.2 of arXiv:1507.02341, compared with the paper's TeX source on 2026-11-26. Collins (1989) was read in full in session 11 (a copy supplied by the director): its Conjecture 9 reads 'The coefficients of CPD(T) for any tree T with n vertices are unimodal with peak between ½n and n(1 − 1/√5)', without floor or ceiling, as arXiv:1507.02341 reports; for odd n the floor is the only reading consistent with Theorem 1 of the same paper (the star peaks at ½(n−1)).

problems.statement: Let $T$ be a tree of order $n \ge 3$ with distance matrix $\mathcal{D}(T)$ (the $(i,j)$ entry is the length of the path from $v_i$ to $v_j$). Let $\delta_k(T)$ be the coefficient of $x^k$ in $\det(\mathcal{D}(T) - xI)$ and, for $0 \le k \le n-2$, let $d_k(T) = 2^{k-(n-2)}\,|\delta_k(T)|$ be the normalized coefficients. Conjecture 1.2 (Collins–Shor), verbatim: "The [normalized] coefficients of the distance characteristic polynomial for any tree $T$ with $n$ vertices are unimodal with peak between $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ and $\lceil n - n/\sqrt{5} \rceil$." Unimodality (indeed log-concavity) is Theorem 2.1 of the same paper. The open part is the location: every index $k$ at which $d_0(T),\dots,d_{n-2}(T)$ attains its maximum satisfies $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor \le k \le \lceil n - n/\sqrt{5} \rceil$. (The source does not say how a tie between two maximal coefficients is to be read; the project uses the strong reading 'every maximizing index' and records ties explicitly.)

problems.name: Chollet's permanent conjecture

source.citation: Chollet (1982), as stated in F. Zhang, An update on a few permanent conjectures, arXiv:1608.02844 (2016), Section 6, inequality (16).
source.statement_number: Chollet conjecture 1982, inequality (16) of the survey
source.note: Statement quoted from Zhang's survey; Chollet's 1982 paper was not accessed.

problems.statement: Quoted from Zhang (arXiv:1608.02844, Section 6 'Chollet conjecture is open'): 'Chollet conjecture 1982 [10]. If A >= 0 and B >= 0 are n x n matrices, then per(A \circ B) <= per A per B (16)'. Here (Zhang, Section 2) M_n is the set of n x n complex matrices, 'A >= 0' means A is positive semidefinite (x^*Ax >= 0 for all x in C^n, hence Hermitian), per A = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \prod_{t=1}^n a_{t\sigma(t)}, and A \circ B = (a_{ij} b_{ij}) is the Hadamard (entrywise) product. Equivalent form (Zhang, quoting Chollet): 'Chollet showed that the inequality holds if and only if it is true when B = \bar{A}: per(A \circ \bar{A}) <= (per A)^2 (17)'. Real special case posed as Zhang's Question 9: for a real positive semidefinite A = (a_{ij}), does per((a_{ij}^2)) <= (per A)^2 hold?

problems.name: Lieb's permanental dominance conjecture

source.citation: E. H. Lieb (1966), as stated in F. Zhang, An update on a few permanent conjectures, arXiv:1608.02844 (2016), Section 4, inequality (10).

problems.statement: Quoted from Zhang (arXiv:1608.02844, Section 4): 'Lieb permanent dominance conjecture 1966 [28]. Let H be a subgroup of the symmetric group S_n and let \chi be a character of degree m of H. Then (1/m) \sum_{\sigma \in H} \chi(\sigma) \prod_{i=1}^n a_{i\sigma(i)} <= per A (10) holds for all n x n positive semidefinite Hermitian A.' Here per A = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \prod_i a_{i\sigma(i)}; the left side is the normalized generalized matrix function d^H_\chi(A)/\chi(e). Important special case (H = S_n, \chi irreducible): every normalized immanant of a PSD matrix is at most its permanent.

problems.name: Liang–So–Zhang per-tensor product conjecture (with Pate's conjecture)

source.citation: Liang, So and Zhang (1992) and Pate (1984), as stated in F. Zhang, An update on a few permanent conjectures, arXiv:1608.02844 (2016), Section 7, inequality (19).
source.note: Statement quoted from Zhang's survey; the primary papers were not accessed and their bibliographic data were not read.

problems.statement: Quoted from Zhang (arXiv:1608.02844, Section 7): 'Liang-So-Zhang per-tensor product conjecture 1992 [59]. Let A and B be n x n and m x m positive semidefinite matrices, respectively. Then (per A)^m (per B)^n <= per(A \otimes B)'. Special case (Pate 1984): 'If M \in M_m is positive semidefinite and J_k is the all one matrix of size k, then (k!)^m (per M)^k <= per(J_k \otimes M) (19) which has been confirmed for k = 2 by Pate 1984 [45] and for m = 2 [59].' For k = 2 the inequality reads 2^m (per M)^2 <= per([[M, M],[M, M]]). Companion conjecture in the same section: 'Liang-So-Zhang Hadamard-Kronecker product conjecture 1992 [59]. Let A and B be n x n positive semidefinite matrices. Then (per(A \circ B))^n <= per(A \otimes B)' (proved in [59, Theorem 2] for any PSD A and special B with all diagonal entries equal and all entries above the main diagonal equal).

problems.name: Ellis–Filmus–Friedgut spectral conjectures H and I for Kneser graphs of downsets

source.citation: D. Ellis, Y. Filmus, E. Friedgut, Chvátal's conjecture: a proof from The Book, arXiv:2609.28404 (v3, 22 October 2026), Section 5, Conjectures H and I.
source.note: The two conjecture sentences were quoted through a summarising fetch and the surrounding definitions are a paraphrase. The PDF must be re-read before any work starts.

problems.statement: Quoted sentences: Conjecture H: "The weighted Hoffman bound is tight for any downset." Conjecture I: "The inertia bound is tight for any downset." Setting (as reported from the paper; wording of the definitions is a close paraphrase obtained through a summarising fetch, not a verbatim copy): a downset is a family $\mathcal{D}\subseteq 2^{[n]}$ with $A\in\mathcal{D},\ B\subseteq A \Rightarrow B\in\mathcal{D}$. $\mathrm{Kn}(\mathcal{D})$ is the graph on vertex set $\mathcal{D}$ in which two sets are adjacent iff they are disjoint (so $\emptyset$ carries a loop). Weighted Hoffman bound: if $M$ is a real symmetric $V\times V$ matrix with $M(x,y)=0$ whenever $xy\notin E(G)$ and $M\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}$, then $\alpha(G)\le \frac{-\lambda_{\min}(M)}{1-\lambda_{\min}(M)}|V(G)|$. Inertia bound: if $M$ is real symmetric with $M(x,y)=0$ whenever $xy\notin E(G)$, then $\alpha(G)\le \#\{\text{nonnegative eigenvalues of } M\}$. 'Tight' is to be read as: for $G=\mathrm{Kn}(\mathcal{D})$ there is an admissible $M$ for which the bound equals the maximum size of an intersecting subfamily of $\mathcal{D}$, which by the (now proved) Chvátal conjecture is the size of the largest star $\max_i |\{A\in\mathcal{D}: i\in A\}|$.

source.citation: Y. Alavi, P. J. Malde, A. J. Schwenk, P. Erdős, The vertex independence sequence of a graph is not constrained, Congr. Numer. 58 (1987) 15-23, Problem 3; quoted via D. Galvin, arXiv:2502.10654.

problems.statement: As quoted in Galvin (arXiv:2502.10654v2) from Alavi–Malde–Schwenk–Erdős, Problem 3: "For trees (or perhaps forests), is the vertex independence sequence unimodal?" Definitions: for a graph G let $i_k(G)$ be the number of independent sets of size k, $0\le k\le \alpha(G)$; the sequence $(i_0,\dots,i_{\alpha(G)})$ (coefficients of the independence polynomial $I(G;x)=\sum_k i_k(G)x^k$) is unimodal if there is m with $i_0\le i_1\le\dots\le i_m\ge i_{m+1}\ge\dots\ge i_{\alpha(G)}$. Conjecture form: the independence polynomial of every tree (resp. forest) is unimodal.

problems.name: Bala's supercongruence conjecture for OEIS A333561

source.citation: P. Bala, comment in OEIS entry A333561 (entry created 27 March 2020; revision 33 of 29 October 2026 read).
source.note: Quoted verbatim from the OEIS entry.

problems.statement:
OEIS A333561, verbatim: 'a(n) = Sum_{j = 0..2*n} binomial(n+j-1,j)*2^j.' ... 'We conjecture that this sequence satisfies the supercongruences a(n*p^k) == a(n*p^(k-1)) ( mod p^(3*k) ) for prime p >= 5 and positive integers n and k. Some examples are given below.'
In LaTeX: with $a(n)=\sum_{j=0}^{2n}\binom{n+j-1}{j}2^j$ ($a(0)=1$; 1, 7, 129, 2815, 65537, 1579007, ...), for every prime $p\ge 5$ and all integers $n,k\ge 1$: $a(np^k)\equiv a(np^{k-1}) \pmod{p^{3k}}$.
Sibling (OEIS A333565, verbatim): 'O.g.f.: (1 + 4*x)/((1 + x)*sqrt(1 - 8*x)).' ... 'We conjecture that this sequence satisfies the stronger congruences a(n*p^k) == a(n*p^(k-1)) ( mod p^(3*k) ) for prime p >= 3 and positive integers n and k. The particular case when n = k = 1 follows from the corresponding result for A333564.'
Further unproved claims in the A333561 entry (easier side targets): 'Conjectural o.g.f.: 1/(1 + x) + 8*x*f'(4*x)/(2*f(4*x) - 1), where f(x) = 1 + x + 3*x^2 + 12*x^3 + 55*x^4 + ... is the o.g.f. of A001764.' and 'exp( Sum_{n >= 1} a(n)*x^n/n ) = 1 + 7*x + 89*x^2 + 1447*x^3 + ... appears to be the o.g.f. of A062747.'

source.citation: Z.-W. Sun, comment in OEIS entry A275027 (12 November 2016; revision 37 of 7 November 2026 read); companion: Conjecture 5.6 of arXiv:1610.03384v8.

problems.name: Kellner's conjectures on denominators of Bernoulli polynomials

source.citation: B. C. Kellner, On the finiteness of Bernoulli polynomials whose derivative has only integral coefficients, J. Integer Seq. 27 (2024), Article 24.2.8, arXiv:2310.01325v2, Conjectures 1(ii), 2(i) and 11; Conjecture 2 originates in B. C. Kellner, J. Number Theory 179 (2017) 126-141.
source.note: Quoted from the fetched arXiv version of the 2024 paper.

problems.statement:
Notation: s_p(n) = sum of the base-p digits of n; rad = radical. Let $D_n^+ := \prod_{p>\sqrt n,\ s_p(n)\ge p} p$ (p prime, n >= 1).
Conjecture 2(i) (Kellner 2017, as restated in 2023): 'We have D_n^+ > 1, respectively, omega(D_n^+) > 0 for n > 192.'
Conjecture 1: with S := {1, 2, 4, 6, 10, 12, 28, 30, 36, 60} and $\bar S := \{n\ge 1 : B_n'(x)\in\mathbb Z[x]\}$ (B_n(x) the Bernoulli polynomials): '(i) The set \bar S is finite. (ii) We have \bar S = S.' Part (i) is now a theorem; part (ii) is open.
Conjecture 11: with $\bar R := \{n\ge 1 : \mathrm{denom}(B_n(x)-B_n) = \mathrm{rad}(n+1)\}$ and R := {3, 5, 8, 9, 11, 27, 29, 35, 59}: 'We have \bar R = R.' (This is the form recorded in OEIS A195441: 'It is conjectured that S = {3, 5, 8, 9, 11, 27, 29, 35, 59} is the full set of all such solutions' of a(n-1) = rad(n+1).)
Logical relations proved in the paper: Conjecture 2(i) implies Conjecture 1(ii) (Theorem 3); Conjecture 11 restricted to odd n implies Conjecture 1 (Theorem 12).

problems.name: Chen–Edelman–Urschel conjecture on the 5x5 growth factor under complete pivoting

source.citation: J. Chen, A. Edelman, J. Urschel, The largest 5th pivot may be the root of a 61st degree polynomial, arXiv:2602.20390v2 (15 March 2026), Conjecture 2.1.
source.note: Quoted from the fetched arXiv page.

problems.statement: Verbatim (arXiv HTML v2): 'Conjecture 2.1. The largest possible growth factor for a $5\times 5$ real matrix under complete pivoting is exactly the lower bound proven in this paper, i.e., the unique real root $g$ in the interval $[4,5]$ of the $61^{st}$ degree polynomial $P_{5}(g)$ in Equation (2.15).' Definitions from the same paper: Gaussian elimination writes $A=LU$; the growth factor is $g(A)=\max\{\|L\|_{\max},\ \|U\|_{\max}/\|A\|_{\max}\}$ where $\|\cdot\|_{\max}$ is the largest magnitude entry. With $A^{(k)}:=A_{k:n,k:n}-A_{k:n,1:k-1}[A_{1:k-1,1:k-1}]^{-1}A_{1:k-1,k:n}$, a matrix is 'completely pivoted' if $|A^{(k)}_{i,j}|\le |A^{(k)}_{k,k}|$ for all $i,j=k,\ldots,n$, $k=1,\ldots,n-1$. For a completely pivoted matrix $g(A)=\max_k |U_{kk}|$, and for the maximum over $n\times n$ completely pivoted matrices it suffices to maximise $|U_{nn}|$. $P_5$ is an explicit integer polynomial of degree 61 printed in Eq. (2.15) of the paper; its relevant root is $g=4.1325170786\,3247285422\,3346853277\,3712699527\ldots$ (200 digits are printed in Eq. (2.16)). Companion statements in the paper, called suppositions rather than numbered conjectures: the lower bounds $5$ for $n=6$, the real root $6.0569534737\ldots$ of $P_7(g)=3g^6-86g^5+688g^4-1136g^3-5888g^2+12032g+22528$ for $n=7$, and $8$ for $n=8$ 'which we suppose are maximums as well'.

source.citation: E. Casas-Alvero, Higher order polar germs, J. Algebra 240 (2001) 326-337; statement quoted from M. F. Marashdeh, arXiv:2608.14726v1 (12 August 2026), Conjecture 1.1.
source.note: Quoted from a 2026 restatement; the 2001 paper was not accessed.

problems.statement: Verbatim from arXiv:2608.14726v1: 'Conjecture 1.1 (Casas-Alvero). Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $0$. Then there is no $\mathrm{CA}$-polynomial over $K$; equivalently, if $f\in K[x]$ is monic of degree $d$ and $\gcd(f,f^{(i)})\neq 1$ for $i=1,\dots,d-1$, then $f=(x-\alpha)^{d}$ for some $\alpha\in K$.' Definition there: for $f(x)=x^{d}+a_{1}x^{d-1}+\cdots+a_{d}\in K[x]$, '$f$ is a Casas-Alvero polynomial (or CA-polynomial) if for every $i\in\{1,\dots,d-1\}$ the polynomial $f$ has a non-constant common factor with its $i$-th Hasse derivative $H_{i}(f)$, and $f$ is not the $d$-th power of a linear polynomial. In characteristic zero $H_{i}(f)=f^{(i)}/i!$'. Target small case: $\mathrm{CA}_{20,0}$, i.e. the statement for $d=20$ ('The smallest degree for which the conjecture is open is $d=20$').
